pages.title: Welcome to CSS course
pages.content:
Take your HTML pages to the next level with CSS. Learn how to style text, control colors, arrange layouts, add animations, and create responsive designs. With hands-on lessons and practical examples, you'll transform plain pages into visually appealing, interactive websites.

---
**What You'll Learn:**

* **CSS Basics:** Understand syntax, selectors, and styling rules.
* **Box Model & Layout:** Control spacing, sizes, and layouts with precision.
* **Typography & Styling:** Customize fonts, text alignment, spacing, and effects.
* **Layout Techniques:** Master Flexbox and CSS Grid to build flexible, modern designs.
* **Interactivity:** Use pseudo-classes, transitions, and transforms to animate and enhance user experience.
* **Responsive Design:** Create websites that look great on all devices using media queries.

**Get ready to turn your HTML knowledge into beautiful, functional websites with CSS!**

pages.title: Introduction to CSS - The Language of Style
pages.content:
- **CSS**, which stands for **C**ascading **S**tyle **S**heets, is the language that adds style to your HTML.
If HTML is like the framework of a house, CSS is the paint, furniture, and decorations. HTML gives your webpage its structure, while CSS gives it its appearance.



---
**The Role of CSS**

The main job of CSS is to control the way your website looks. This includes:
* **Colors:** Changing the colors of text, backgrounds, and buttons.
* **Layout:** Deciding where elements go on the page. Do you want things side-by-side or stacked on top of each other?
* **Fonts:** Choosing different font styles, sizes, and weights for your text.

The best practice is to keep your CSS separate from your HTML. This makes your code more organized and efficient. For example, if you want to change the color of all the headings on your website, you can do it with just one line of code in your CSS file.

Now you have a basic understanding of what CSS is for. In the next lesson, we will start learning about how to write CSS and connect it to your HTML files.

pages.title: Applying CSS - Inline
pages.content:
- When you want to quickly style just one element on a webpage, you can use **inline CSS**.  
- With inline CSS, the style is written **directly inside the HTML tag** using the `style` attribute.  
Think of it like writing a sticky note on one element saying “Hey, look different!”.

**Good for:** quick changes, testing, or when you only need to style one element.  
**Not good for:** large projects, because your HTML becomes messy and hard to manage.

For example:
```afefc
This is styled with inline CSS.
```

pages.title: CSS Syntax
pages.content:
- CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) uses a simple and consistent **syntax** to style HTML elements. Every CSS rule has **three main parts**:



---
**1. Selector**
- The **selector** tells the browser *which HTML element(s)* you want to style.\
 Example: `p` selects all `` tags.\
 Example: `.title` selects all elements with class="title".

**2. Property**
- The **property** defines *what aspect* of the element you want to style.\
  Examples: `color`, `font-size`, `background`, `margin`.

**3. Value**
- The **value** specifies *how the property should be applied*.\
  Examples: `red`, `20px`, `center`, `bold`.

---
**Example Rule**

```css
p {
   color: blue;
   font-size: 18px;
}
```

This means: *"Make all `` text blue, with a font size of 18px."*

pages.title: CSS Selectors
pages.content:
- You've already learned to use a simple **element selector**, like `p`, to style every single paragraph on a page. That's great for global changes, but what if you want to style some paragraphs differently from others? Or what if you want to target a single, unique element?
- To do that, you need to use more specific selectors. This is where **universal**, **class**, and **ID** selectors come in. They give you the power to target and style elements with precision.

---
**1. The Element Selector (`p`,`h1`, `div`)**\
This is the selector you already know. It targets all elements of a specific type.

* **When to use it:** To style every instance of a specific HTML tag. For example, to make all `` tags blue or all `` links a certain color.
* **Syntax:** Just the name of the HTML tag.\
CSS
```css
p {
  color: darkgreen;
}
```
---

**2. The Class Selector (`.`)**\
Think of a class as a **category**. You can give a class name to as many HTML elements as you want. Any element that has that class name will receive the styles you apply to it.

* **When to use it:** To style **multiple elements** that share a common purpose or appearance. For example, you might have a class called `highlight` to make certain words stand out, or a class called `card` to style a group of different boxes on your page.
* **Syntax:** You start the selector with a period (`.`) followed by the class name you choose.

CSS

```css
.card {
  background-color: lightgray;
}
```
---
**3. The ID Selector (`#`)**\
Think of an ID as a **unique identifier**, like a Social Security number. An ID can only be used **once** on an entire web page.

* **When to use it:** To style a **single, unique element**. You might use an ID for a main navigation bar, a specific logo, or a hero image that only appears once.
* **Syntax:** You start the selector with a hash symbol (`#`) followed by the ID name you choose.

CSS

```css
#main-heading {
  font-size: 32px;
  color: navy;
}
```
---
**4. The Universal Selector (`*`)**\
Think of the universal selector as a way to select **everything**. It is the most general selector and is often used to apply a style to all elements on the page.

* **When to use it:** To apply a default style to every element, such as setting a consistent font, or to reset padding and margins at the beginning of a stylesheet.
* **Syntax:** It is a single asterisk (`*`).

CSS

```css
* {
  font-size: 16px;
}
```
